q: When should a coding agent ask a stronger model for help?
alt: When do I consult instead of just working?
a: Only on a trigger. Drake's agents consult when (1) two different fixes failed or the root cause is unknown, (2) the next step is hard to reverse (merge, delete, gate or protocol change, stopping a live service), (3) results contradict or a number surprises by more than its noise, or (4) the agent is about to call something done or safe and is not sure. Never for routine edits or anything one more tool call settles. You can run his rule: `sh examples/agents-01-roles-and-models/run.sh`.

q: Why use two consultants instead of one?
alt: What does Drake do at a real fork?
How do I get independent opinions from models?
a: For a real fork between approaches, Drake spawns two consultants in one batch with the **same facts and file paths and without his worker's conclusion**. Where they agree, act. Where they disagree, run the cheapest check that separates them, or take the choice to the person who owns it with both positions. A fresh context is another reading; it does not prove the two are different models, so check what each role resolved to.

q: What roles does Drake give his agents?
alt: How is Drake's agent setup organized?
Which models does Drake use for what?
a: In general terms: one default worker model for all lanes, read-only consultant roles backed by stronger models for hard or irreversible calls, reviewer and security-reviewer agents, and a roster of advisor seats that read each run at the end. His harness, omp, also has fast and slow roles (`--smol`, `--slow`). The point is that roles stay boring so you always know what produced a change.

q: What is a SKILL.md?
alt: How do skills work in omp or Claude Code?
a: A skill is a directory `skills/<name>/` holding `SKILL.md`: a `---` frontmatter block with `name` (equal to the directory) and `description`, then a body of checks. Agents read every description at startup and load the full body only when the task matches, so the description must say **when** to use it. Drake pins each claim to a source commit and records verified example output.

q: How should I install the omega-harness skills?
alt: How do I keep skills up to date?
a: Clone https://github.com/aien-dev/omega-harness and link each skill directory into your agent's skill directory (or point omp's custom skill directories at the clone). Then `git pull` updates every agent. A copy is a snapshot that silently goes stale. The example `examples/agents-02-skills/run.sh` shows a symlinked install reading v2 after a pull while a copy still reads v1.

q: How can I check that a skill's frontmatter is valid?
alt: Why does my skill never load?
a: Run `check-skill.sh SKILL_DIR` from the lesson: line 1 must be `---`, the block must close, `name` must equal the directory, and `description` must say when to use it. Drake's six skills pass; the three malformed controls (wrong name, no 'Use ...', no frontmatter) fail with exit 1. A description that never says when is the usual reason a skill never loads.

q: Can an agent review its own work?
alt: Who should check an agent's change?
a: Not as the only check. Drake's rule is 'the witness verifies and touches nothing': a separate read-only reviewer reads the diff and the evidence, a security reviewer looks for trust problems, and advisor seats read the finished run. A model review still is not a receipt; it tells you where to look.

q: Two reviewers disagree. What do I do?
alt: How do I weigh conflicting reviews?
a: Per finding: both say defect with evidence, **act**; they disagree with evidence, **check** (run the cheapest command that separates the two readings); only one gives evidence, **verify** the cited artifact yourself; nobody gives evidence, **drop** it. Confidence is not evidence. Try `sh examples/agents-03-reviewers-and-advisors/run.sh`.

q: What are advisor seats?
alt: What does the witness seat do?
How does Drake's advisor roster work?
a: Advisors read a whole run when it ends, each holding one office: intent (is this what was asked?), a witness with read-only tools (where is the artifact behind each claim of done, PASS, merged or measured?), numbers (recompute in Wolfram, require MEASURED or MODELED labels), direction (is new code going into Omega?), and trust (could this mislead, was an outside effect taken without approval?). Each speaks only with concrete evidence and stays silent otherwise.

q: How do I run several coding agents on one repository?
alt: How does Drake split work into lanes?
a: One lane, one isolated tree: each agent gets its own git worktree or clone on its own branch. Every shared surface gets exactly one integration owner who merges committed branches only. No agent ever checks out, resets, stashes or cleans in another agent's tree. The demo `examples/agents-04-lanes-and-integration/run.sh` shows four lanes and an owner.

q: What should the integration owner do on a merge conflict?
a: Abort the merge so the shared branch stays clean, and send the conflict back to the lane that owns the change. That lane rebases in its own worktree and decides, then the owner merges again. The owner does not know why the lane changed that line; the lane does.

q: How do agents coordinate on directories?
alt: How do agents avoid editing the same directory?
a: Through the repository. Drake's repos carry a committed `.crumb` per directory that states its purpose and invariants, plus an ignored local file for locks and in-progress notes. Agents read the crumb and check for a lock before editing. Before starting a lane, they also search the whole organization for prior work.

q: How should an agent record what it learned?
a: One distilled lesson per entry: **Symptom** (what you saw), **Root cause**, **Fix** (one targeted change), **Verified** (command, status, negative control, source commit). Not files, not chat logs. Drake's validator `lesson.om` refuses an entry without a usable Verified line: `sh examples/agents-05-memory-and-lessons/run.sh`.

q: Can I trust what an agent remembers?
alt: Memory says X but the code says Y
a: Memory is navigation, not proof. A recalled lesson tells you where to look; you still read the current source and run the check. When memory and the repository disagree, the repository wins and the memory gets corrected.

q: What do I do with a lesson that turned out wrong?
alt: How to fix bad agent memory
a: Retract that entry by its id and record the corrected lesson. Do not add a second lesson that contradicts the first, because the next agent would have to guess which is true. For receipts it is the same idea: add a correction beside the old record, never rewrite it.

q: How does Drake correct an agent?
alt: How do I redirect a coding agent?
a: In a sentence or two: name what the agent did, the principle it missed, and the next concrete action. When the same correction keeps coming back, it moves into the shared rules or a skill, so it costs nothing next time. His recurring ones are on the steer cards: look facts up, verify with your own tools, a missing piece is a task, aim for the limit, search before you claim.

q: What does 'fix it, don't file it' mean?
alt: Should an agent file an issue or fix the bug?
a: A defect you can reproduce is a defect you can fix, in the same piece of work, even in someone else's lane. Filing an issue alone leaves the work unfinished. Stop only for a real external gate (authorization you do not have, a decision that is the owner's, a check you genuinely exhausted) and name it. Check a report with `sh examples/agents-06-correcting-agents/run.sh`.

q: My agent keeps asking me to check things. What should I tell it?
alt: Agent hands verification to the human
a: If its tools can verify it, it verifies it. It exhausts its own tools (logs, device state, the network, existing instructions) and then asks you only for the smallest observation or physical action tools cannot reach, stating the exact access limit.

q: My test runner says 0 failed. Is that a pass?
a: Not by itself. Fix the expected case count before the run and compare: fewer results than expected means cases were lost (a shrinking denominator), and NOT_RUN or SKIP is not PASS. In the lesson, all four logs have zero FAIL lines and only one passes. Run `sh examples/agents-07-failure-patterns/run.sh`.

q: What are the most common ways agents overclaim?
a: Receipts with no artifact; runners that silently lose cases; NOT_RUN counted as PASS; a successful compile taken as working behavior; merged called deployed or a host run called hardware-qualified; and a lead restoring a setting before its child agent actually started. Each has a check: open the artifact, fix the denominator, run the changed path with a negative control, use the narrowest true status.

q: Is a successful compile evidence that code works?
a: No. Compile success shows nothing about behavior. Run the changed path, compare expected and observed output and status, and run a negative control that must fail. A checker that never rejected anything has not shown it can.

q: What should I put in a brief for another agent?
alt: How to hand off work to an agent
a: Six parts: goal, non-goals, authority (what it may and may not touch), the exact source commit (not a branch), the contract and acceptance command, and the evidence it must send back (commit, commands, statuses, output, negative control, what was not run). Never a chat dump. Try `sh examples/agents-08-evidence-handoff/run.sh`.

q: Why not just reference the branch name?
alt: Branch or commit in a handoff?
a: A branch moves between the brief and the work, so two agents can read different code under the same name. A commit is exact. Drake's checker holds a handoff whose Source line has no commit.

q: What should an agent's report back look like?
alt: What does a good status report contain?
a: Lead with the outcome and its scope, then the revision and target, the concrete change, the evidence (exact commands, expected versus observed, negative control, where the receipt lives) and the limits: what was not run, open risks, the next decision needed. Use the narrowest true status: proposed, implemented, exercised, qualified, merged, deployed.

q: Who updates the documentation when an agent changes the code?
a: The agent that made the change, in the same piece of work. Drake keeps a map from each kind of change to the skill that must absorb it. A task that changes something a guide describes is not done until the guide matches. If the agent cannot update it, it opens an issue saying exactly what is stale.

q: How do I update a guide correctly?
alt: Updating a skill after a change
a: Replace the rule the change made untrue (do not append a contradicting note), give the new source commit and date, rerun any changed example against the new pin and record what you observed, then open the guide PR linked to the change, as a draft if the change is not merged yet. Never rewrite old receipts.

q: Can this be checked automatically?
alt: Detect stale docs in a diff
a: Partly. The lesson's `guides.om` reads `git diff --name-only` and flags a change under `compiler/` that did not touch its guide. It catches the forgotten update, not a wrong one. Run `sh examples/agents-09-keeping-guides-current/run.sh`.
